headline: Futures edge higher and the 10-year yield sits near 4.60% after July's payrolls contraction flipped September pricing toward a hold, while Brent trades near $84.50 with the Hormuz reopening still unproven.
stance: The question the market takes into this week inverted on Friday: the economy shed 23,000 jobs in July against forecasts near an 83,000 gain — June was revised down to a 20,000 increase — and by Sunday afternoon prediction-market pricing put 65% odds on the Fed holding at the September 16 meeting, with a quarter-point hike near 33% versus roughly 62% midweek. Equities chose the rate relief over the growth message, closing Friday higher with yields down. The unresolved piece is oil: Iran said its Oman shipping-route agreement is in "final stages" while conditioning any Hormuz reopening on further US concessions, attacks resumed on the Red Sea port of Mocha, and Brent traded near $84.50 early Monday — about $2 above Friday's close. Wednesday's consumer-price report (forecast +0.1% headline, +0.2% core) is the test of whether the hold case survives the energy pass-through.

news.head: Jobs shock: payrolls fell 23,000 in July
news.body: Friday's employment report showed the economy shed 23,000 jobs in July, against forecasts near an 83,000 gain, and June was revised down to a 20,000 increase from the 57,000 first reported. The unemployment rate came in at 4.1%, versus expectations it would hold at 4.2%.

news.head: September repriced within hours
news.body: Midweek pricing had implied roughly 62% odds of a quarter-point hike at the September 16 meeting; by Sunday afternoon, prediction-market pricing put about 65% odds on the Fed holding and roughly 33% on a hike. Treasury yields fell Friday — the 2-year closed at 4.19% from 4.25% Thursday, the 10-year at 4.65% from 4.69% — and the 10-year traded near 4.60% early Monday (~4am ET).

news.head: Stocks took it as relief
news.body: The S&P 500 closed Friday up 0.6% at 7,757.64, the Dow up 0.3% at 54,036.93, and the Nasdaq up 1.3% at 26,690.62 — the tape read the weak print as rate relief rather than a growth alarm. Early Monday (~4am ET), S&P 500 futures were up about 0.1%, Nasdaq futures up about 0.3–0.4%, and Dow futures little changed.

news.head: Hormuz: "final stages," with conditions
news.body: Iran said over the weekend that its agreement with Oman on new shipping routes is in "final stages" but that the strait reopens only if the US meets further conditions; the US Treasury secretary countered that redirected pipeline flows would make the strait "irrelevant," and Houthi attacks resumed on the Red Sea port of Mocha. Brent traded near $84.50 early Monday (~4am ET), about $2 above Friday's $82.27 close, with US crude near $79 against a $77.08 Friday close.

news.head: Gold closes at the top of its range
news.body: Gold reversed Friday's early dip — from about $4,292 early Friday to a $4,401 close, near the top of its three-year range — and held around $4,400 overnight (~4am ET). Silver closed Friday at $63.80, up from about $61.60 early Friday.

news.head: Friday's insider filings: two new clusters
news.body: Filings dated Friday show seven distinct insiders at BRVE buying about $3.9 million of stock and five at ATTO about $2.7 million — the two largest new clusters in the newest filings, following the midweek pharma buying already covered last week.

implications: The September call now leans hold, but it is oil's to flip: hike odds fell from about 62% midweek to roughly 33% by Sunday, and Wednesday's consumer-price report — forecast +0.1% headline, +0.2% core — is the first test of whether the energy shock is reaching prices faster than the labor market is cooling.

The bond rally has contrarian fuel behind it: the latest weekly futures data shows speculators newly flipped to extended short in 10-year Treasury futures (the 12th percentile of the past three years) — extended shorts are potential buyers if yields keep falling — while the long-standing extended-long position in 2-year futures was finally rewarded by Friday's drop in short yields.

Equities carry a contrarian cushion into the inflation number: bullish bets on Nasdaq 100 futures sit at the 1st percentile of the past three years even after Friday's 1.3% Nasdaq gain — skepticism, not euphoria, is the backdrop — though with the VIX closing Friday at 14.9, little hedging is in place if Wednesday's report runs hot.

The dollar is the newly exposed trade: speculators went extended long the dollar index (90th percentile, new this week) just as the jobs miss knocked the currency — the yen firmed from about ¥158.5 per dollar early Friday to ¥157.75 at Friday's close — and Japan's finance minister said authorities "would not hesitate" to intervene again.

watch.head: Proof on the strait
watch.body: What settles the oil question is evidence rather than statements: free tanker movement through Hormuz or a documented, published agreement. Until one appears, the weekend attacks near Mocha argue the risk premium stays in crude.

watch.head: First Fed voice after the print
watch.body: Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack appears today — the first scheduled read on how officials weigh a shrinking payroll count against oil back above $84 ahead of the September 16 meeting.

watch.head: Wednesday's consumer-price report
watch.body: Forecasts center on +0.1% headline and +0.2% core. With hold odds near 65%, a hot reading — particularly visible energy pass-through — is what would put the September hike back on the table; July retail sales follow Friday (forecast +0.2%).

watch.head: Today's and this week's calendar
watch.body: Simon Property Group reports after today's close; Applied Materials, Cisco and CoreWeave are scheduled later this week — the first broad earnings test of whether the rate-relief rally extends.

sections.title: Macro & Rates
bullets: The biggest change since Friday morning: the July employment report showed the economy shed 23,000 jobs — forecasts were near an 83,000 gain — with June revised down to a 20,000 increase and the unemployment rate at 4.1%. The number the whole week pointed at landed on the other side of zero.

Rates repriced immediately: the 2-year Treasury yield closed Friday at 4.19% (4.25% Thursday), the 10-year at 4.65% (4.69%), steepening the curve slightly to +46 basis points from +44 — and the 10-year traded near 4.60% early Monday (~4am ET). By Sunday afternoon, prediction-market pricing put about 65% odds on the Fed holding on September 16 and roughly 33% on a quarter-point hike, versus roughly 62% hike odds midweek.

Inflation compensation barely moved on the jobs news: the 10-year breakeven rate closed Friday at 2.25% (2.26% Thursday) with the 10-year real, inflation-adjusted yield at 2.40% (2.43% Thursday) — the bond market is treating this as a growth story for now, with the oil test still ahead.

The yen strengthened through Friday's session after the data — from about ¥158.5 per dollar early Friday to ¥157.75 at the close, touching ¥156.68 intraday — and Japan's finance minister said authorities "would not hesitate" to step in again after the prior week's joint intervention. The dollar index closed Friday at 99.6, the euro at $1.156, and the pound at $1.3493 — a fresh upper extreme for the pound, in the 86th percentile of its three-year range.

Brent settled Friday at $82.27, easing from Thursday's $82.49, then gapped higher over the weekend to trade near $84.50 early Monday (~4am ET) as the reopening stayed unproven; US crude closed Friday at $77.08 and traded near $79 overnight.

Gold reversed Friday's early dip — about $4,292 early Friday to a $4,401.30 close, a fresh extreme near the top of its three-year range (86th percentile) — and held near $4,400 overnight; silver closed Friday at $63.80, up from about $61.60 early Friday.
sections.positioning: New in the latest weekly futures data (positions as of Tuesday): speculators flipped to extended short in 10-year Treasury futures — the 12th percentile of the past three years, a contrarian-bullish lean, since extended shorts are potential buyers if yields keep falling — and went extended long both the dollar index (90th percentile) and gold (87th percentile), contrarian-bearish leans that Friday's post-jobs dollar slide already began to test. Standing background, not new: the extended-long position in 2-year Treasury futures sits at the 100th percentile of the past three years — the market's most stretched bet that short rates fall, and Friday finally paid it.

sections.title: Equity Markets
bullets: Friday's close: S&P 500 up 0.6% at 7,757.64, Dow up 0.3% at 54,036.93, Nasdaq up 1.3% at 26,690.62 — a rate-relief rally on a payrolls contraction. Early Monday (~4am ET), S&P 500 futures were up about 0.1%, Nasdaq futures up about 0.3–0.4%, and Dow futures little changed.
Volatility went home lower on jobs day: the VIX closed Friday at 14.9, down from 15.2 Thursday — thin protection in place ahead of Wednesday's consumer-price report.
Breadth improved at Friday's close: about 68% of S&P 500 members traded above their 50-day trend line (roughly 65% Thursday), and 62% of Nasdaq-100 members did (55% Thursday).
Friday's newest insider filings added two clusters: seven distinct buyers at BRVE totaling about $3.9 million and five at ATTO totaling about $2.7 million — the two largest in the newest filings.
sections.positioning: New in the latest weekly futures data: speculators' net position in Nasdaq 100 futures fell to the 1st percentile of the past three years — almost no bullish bets outstanding — with hedgers at the opposite extreme, a contrarian-bullish divergence. In plain English: the fast money came into Friday's 1.3% Nasdaq gain positioned against it, and positioning that one-sided means much of the potential selling is already sold.

single_name.note: (American Bitcoin Corp., a finance-services name) — a fresh insider purchase was filed Friday, the shares trade above their 200-day trend line, and the setup's dark-pool and options signals are both live; it joined the scan list Friday with a top score.

sections.title: Credit & Liquidity
bullets: Credit shrugged at the growth scare, at least through Thursday (spread data runs a day behind): the high-yield-over-investment-grade spread narrowed to 271 basis points at Thursday's close from 275 Wednesday, with investment-grade spreads steady at 78 basis points.
Bond-market volatility sits low for a jobs-shock week: the MOVE index — the Treasury market's version of the VIX — closed Friday at 72.

Short-term funding stayed quiet through the data: the key bank-funding spreads closed Thursday near 2 basis points, and the commercial-paper funding spread eased to 20 basis points Friday from 22 earlier in the week.

The system's spare-cash cushion remains gone: the overnight reverse-repo facility held $1.4 billion Friday, with bank reserves at $2,993.3 billion and the Treasury's cash account at $907.3 billion in Wednesday's weekly snapshot. Bank credit grew 6.2% year-over-year in the late-July weekly reading, and the average rate on new syndicated loans sat at 7.1%.
sections.positioning: Primary-dealer high-yield inventory sits mid-range — the 35th percentile of its three-year span in the weekly dealer data — no stress signal on either side of the credit book.
